title: Area and Circumference of Circles Flashcards

cards.front: Name the line segment that goes from the centre of a circle to its edge.
cards.back: Radius

options.explanation: A radius is a line segment joining the centre of a circle to any point on its circumference.
A diameter extends from one edge to the opposite edge through the centre. The segment from the centre to one edge is the radius.
A chord joins two points on the circumference and does not have to pass through the centre. A radius joins the centre to the circle’s edge.
A tangent is a straight line touching the circle at exactly one point. A radius is the segment running from the centre to the edge.

cards.front: Name the straight line that passes through the centre from edge to edge.
cards.back: Diameter

options.explanation: A diameter is a straight line segment joining two points on the circumference and passing through the centre of the circle.
A radius runs only from the centre to one edge, so it is half this length. The full edge-to-edge line through the centre is the diameter.
A tangent touches the circumference at only one point and does not cross the circle. The edge-to-edge line through the centre is the diameter.
An arc is a curved section of the circumference, not a straight line through the circle. The required straight line is the diameter.

cards.front: What is the name for a straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point?
cards.back: Tangent

options.explanation: A tangent is a straight line that meets a circle at exactly one point, called the point of contact.
A chord has both endpoints on the circumference, so it meets the circle at two points. A line touching at exactly one point is a tangent.
A secant passes through a circle and intersects its circumference at two points. A straight line meeting it at only one point is a tangent.
A radius is a segment from the centre to the circumference, rather than a line touching the circle externally. The required line is a tangent.

cards.front: Name the part of a circle formed by two radii and an arc.
cards.back: Sector

options.explanation: A sector is the region enclosed by two radii and the arc connecting their endpoints, resembling a slice of a circle.
A segment is enclosed by a chord and an arc, not by two radii. The region enclosed by two radii and an arc is a sector.
An arc is only a curved portion of the circumference and does not include an enclosed area. Two radii and an arc enclose a sector.
A chord is a straight line segment joining two points on the circumference. The area bounded by two radii and an arc is a sector.

cards.front: The diameter is twice the length of the [ ___ ] ($d = 2r$).
cards.back: The diameter is twice the length of the radius ($d = 2r$).

options.explanation: The diameter crosses the full width of the circle through its centre, while the radius covers half that distance, so $d = 2r$.
This incorrectly says the diameter is twice itself. The diameter is twice the radius because two radii placed end to end form a diameter.
The circumference is the distance around the circle, not half its diameter. The diameter is twice the radius, giving the relationship $d = 2r$.
A chord can have many different lengths depending on its position, so the diameter is not always twice a chord. It is specifically twice the radius.

cards.front: The [ ___ ] is the total distance all the way around the edge of a circle.
cards.back: The circumference is the total distance all the way around the edge of a circle.

options.explanation: The circumference is the complete distance around the curved boundary of a circle, equivalent to the perimeter of the circle.
Area measures the two-dimensional space enclosed inside a circle, not the distance around its edge. The total distance around the edge is the circumference.
The diameter is a straight distance across the circle through its centre. The total distance around the circle’s curved edge is the circumference.
The radius measures from the centre to one point on the edge, rather than all the way around it. The distance around the edge is the circumference.

cards.front: State the formula for circumference using the diameter ($d$).
cards.back: $$C = \pi d$

options.explanation: A circle’s circumference is found by multiplying its diameter by $\pi$, so the formula using diameter is $C = \pi d$.
The factor of $2$ is used when the formula contains the radius, because $d = 2r$. Using diameter directly gives $C = \pi d$.
Dividing by $2$ confuses the diameter with the radius and produces only half the circumference. Using the diameter directly, the correct formula is $C = \pi d$.
Squaring a length is associated with area, not circumference, and this expression also lacks the area formula’s factor of one quarter. Circumference is $C = \pi d$.

cards.front: State the formula for circumference using the radius ($r$).
cards.back: $$C = 2\pi r$

options.explanation: Since the diameter equals $2r$ and $C = \pi d$, substituting $d = 2r$ gives the radius form $C = 2\pi r$.
This misses the factor of $2$ needed to convert the radius into the diameter, so it gives half the circumference. The correct formula is $C = 2\pi r$.
Squaring the radius changes the quantity from a length to an area, so this cannot represent circumference. The correct linear formula is $C = 2\pi r$.
This is the formula for the area enclosed by a circle, not the distance around its edge. The circumference using radius is $C = 2\pi r$.

cards.front: For decimal answers, use the [ ___ ] on your calculator unless instructed otherwise.
cards.back: For decimal answers, use the $\pi$ button on your calculator unless instructed otherwise.

options.explanation: The $\pi$ button uses the calculator’s stored value of pi, giving greater accuracy than entering a rounded approximation such as 3.14.
The $x^2$ button squares a number and does not enter pi. The $\pi$ button should be used to obtain accurate decimal answers involving circles.
The square root button finds the number that was squared; it does not enter pi. Circle calculations require the $\pi$ button for accurate decimal answers.
The EXP button enters powers of ten in standard form, not the circle constant. The $\pi$ button provides the accurate value needed for circle calculations.

cards.front: State the formula for the area of a circle.

options.explanation: A circle’s area is found by squaring its radius and multiplying by pi, so the correct formula is $A = \pi r^2$.
This is the formula for circumference, not area. Area measures the space inside the circle and is calculated using $A = \pi r^2$.
This omits the essential step of squaring the radius. The area of a circle is calculated using $A = \pi r^2$.
This incorrectly squares the diameter as though it were the radius. The correct formula uses the radius: $A = \pi r^2$.

cards.front: What must be done to the diameter before it can be used in the area formula $A = \pi r^2$?
cards.back: Halve it to find the radius ($r = \frac{d}{2}$).

options.text: Halve it to find the radius ($r = \frac{d}{2}$).
options.explanation: The radius is half the diameter, so the diameter must be divided by 2 before substituting into the area formula $A = \pi r^2$.

options.text: Double it to find the radius ($r = 2d$).
options.explanation: This reverses the relationship between radius and diameter. The diameter is twice the radius, so it must be halved: $r = \frac{d}{2}$.

options.text: Square it to find the radius ($r = d^2$).
options.explanation: Squaring is applied to the radius within the area formula, not when converting diameter to radius. First use $r = \frac{d}{2}$.

options.text: Use it directly as the radius ($r = d$).
options.explanation: This confuses the diameter with the radius and makes the calculated area four times too large. The diameter must first be halved using $r = \frac{d}{2}$.

cards.front: Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 16 mm in terms of $\pi$.
cards.back: $$16\pi$ mm

options.explanation: Circumference can be calculated using $C = \pi d$. Substituting the diameter of 16 mm gives $C = \pi \times 16 = 16\pi$ mm.
This unnecessarily halves the diameter before using $C = \pi d$. Since the given diameter is 16 mm, the circumference is $16\pi$ mm.
This doubles the diameter, confusing $C = \pi d$ with the equivalent radius formula $C = 2\pi r$. The correct circumference is $16\pi$ mm.
This squares the diameter, incorrectly applying an area-style calculation to circumference. Using $C = \pi d$ gives a circumference of $16\pi$ mm.

cards.front: Find the area of a circle with radius 9 cm in terms of $\pi$.

options.explanation: Using $A = \pi r^2$ with $r = 9$ gives $A = \pi \times 9^2 = 81\pi$ $cm^2$.
This uses $2\pi r$, which calculates circumference rather than area. Squaring the radius in $A = \pi r^2$ gives $81\pi$ $cm^2$.
This multiplies the radius by pi without squaring it. Since $9^2 = 81$, the correct area is $81\pi$ $cm^2$.
This doubles the correct area, often from adding an unnecessary factor of 2. The formula is $A = \pi r^2$, giving $81\pi$ $cm^2$.

cards.front: Identify the two components needed to calculate the total perimeter of a semi-circle.
cards.back: Half the circumference (the arc)The diameter (straight edge)

options.text: Half the circumference (the arc)The diameter (straight edge)
options.explanation: A semi-circle’s boundary consists of the curved arc, which is half a full circumference, and the straight diameter joining the arc’s endpoints.

options.text: Half the area (the inside)The diameter (straight edge)
options.explanation: Area measures the surface inside a shape and cannot form part of its perimeter. The required components are half the circumference and the diameter.

options.text: All the circumference (the arc)The radius (straight edge)
options.explanation: A semi-circle has only half the circle’s curved circumference, and its straight edge spans two radii. The components are half the circumference and the diameter.

options.text: Half the circumference (the arc)The radius (straight edge)
options.explanation: The curved part is correctly identified, but the straight edge runs across the entire circle and is therefore the diameter, not a single radius.

cards.front: A [ ___ ] is exactly one half of a circle.
cards.back: A semi-circle is exactly one half of a circle.

options.explanation: A semi-circle is formed when a circle is divided into two equal parts, so it represents exactly one half of the original circle.
A quadrant is one quarter of a circle rather than one half. A shape representing exactly half of a circle is called a semi-circle.
A sector is a region enclosed by two radii and an arc, and its size can vary. Exactly half a circle is specifically a semi-circle.
A quarter-circle represents one of four equal parts, not one of two equal parts. Exactly one half of a circle is a semi-circle.

cards.front: An [ ___ ] is defined as a part of the circle's circumference.
cards.back: An arc is defined as a part of the circle's circumference.

options.explanation: An arc is a section of a circle’s curved boundary, so it is defined as part of the circle’s circumference.
An angle measures the amount of turn between two lines and is not part of a circle’s circumference. A section of the circumference is an arc.
Area measures the region enclosed inside a circle rather than part of its boundary. A part of the circle’s circumference is called an arc.
An annulus is the region between two concentric circles, not a section of one circle’s circumference. Such a section is called an arc.

cards.front: Explain the strategy for finding the shaded area between a large circle and a smaller circle inside it.
cards.back: Subtract the area of the smaller circle from the area of the larger circle.

options.text: Subtract the area of the smaller circle from the area of the larger circle.
options.explanation: The shaded region is the part of the larger circle not occupied by the smaller circle, so its area is found using larger area minus smaller area.

options.text: Add the area of the smaller circle to the area of the larger circle.
options.explanation: Adding counts the inner circle as extra area rather than removing it. The shaded area is the larger circle’s area minus the smaller circle’s area.

options.text: Subtract the area of the larger circle from the area of the smaller circle.
options.explanation: Reversing the subtraction produces a negative value because the larger circle has greater area. Subtract the smaller circle’s area from the larger circle’s area.

options.text: Divide the area of the larger circle by the area of the smaller circle.
options.explanation: Division gives a ratio between the two areas, not the area of the shaded region. Find each area, then subtract the smaller from the larger.

cards.front: When calculating the number of boxes or bags needed to cover an area, always [ ___ ] to the nearest whole number.
cards.back: When calculating the number of boxes or bags needed to cover an area, always round up to the nearest whole number.

options.explanation: A fraction of a box or bag cannot usually be purchased, so any non-whole result must be increased to the next whole number to ensure enough coverage.
Rounding down would leave part of the area uncovered whenever the calculation is not a whole number. The required number must therefore be rounded up.
Ordinary rounding can reduce values with decimal parts below $0.5$, leaving insufficient materials. Boxes or bags must always be rounded up to the next whole number.
Truncating simply removes the decimal part, which gives too few boxes or bags for complete coverage. The result must instead be rounded up.

cards.front: How do you calculate the total cost for fencing a circular field?
cards.back: Calculate the circumferenceMultiply the circumference by the cost per metre

options.text: Calculate the circumferenceMultiply the circumference by the cost per metre
options.explanation: Fencing follows the boundary of the circular field, so the required length is its circumference. Multiplying this length by the cost per metre gives the total cost.

options.text: Calculate the areaMultiply the area by the cost per metre
options.explanation: Area measures the surface inside the field, not the boundary being fenced. Calculate the circumference, then multiply it by the fencing cost per metre.

options.text: Calculate the circumferenceDivide the circumference by the cost per metre
options.explanation: Dividing length by a price per metre does not produce a monetary cost. Multiply the circumference by the cost per metre to obtain the total.

options.text: Calculate the diameterMultiply the diameter by the cost per metre
options.explanation: The diameter crosses the field once and is not the full boundary length. Fencing requires the circumference, which is multiplied by the cost per metre.

cards.front: What are the standard units for the area of a circle?
cards.back: Square units (e.g., $cm^2$ or $m^2$)

options.explanation: Area measures a two-dimensional surface, so its units are squared. Circle areas are therefore expressed in square units such as $cm^2$ or $m^2$.
Linear units measure one-dimensional quantities such as radius or circumference. Because area is two-dimensional, it must use square units such as $cm^2$ or $m^2$.
Cubic units measure three-dimensional volume, not the surface of a circle. Circle area is measured in square units such as $cm^2$ or $m^2$.
Degrees and radians measure angles rather than area. The area of a circle is a two-dimensional quantity measured in square units such as $cm^2$ or $m^2$.
